slides: Let's continue with what is always true, and a special kind of choice.

slides.say: Now, questions about what is always true, or not always true. To show that something is not always true, one example where it fails is enough.

For example, is a squared plus b squared always equal to the bracket a plus b, squared? Let a equal one and b equal two, two small, easy numbers. One plus four is five, and three squared is nine. Five is not nine, so it's not always true. One counterexample, and we're done.

But always is different. A few examples that work don't prove always, because the next number might fail. In a question with choices, we don't prove it. We rule out the other three choices, and the one that's left is the answer.

Some questions have a choice that says cannot be determined. That means the givens don't fix one answer. Another choice you may see is none of the above is necessarily true. That means none of the listed statements is true in every allowed case.
One working example doesn't rule out either kind of choice. Why? Because another allowed example might give a different result, or make the statement false. We need to look beyond that one example.
at: One working example doesn't rule out

slides.say: For example, given: x is not equal to zero. Which of the following is necessarily true? Choice number one, x squared is greater than or equal to x. Choice number two, x squared is smaller than x. Choice number three, x squared is equal to x. And choice number four, none of the above is necessarily true.
Necessarily true means true for every allowed x. So one x where a choice is false rules it out. Zero isn't allowed, so the easiest number is one. One squared is one.
Choice number one says x squared is greater than or equal to x. One is equal to one, so it stays. Choice number two says x squared is smaller than x. One isn't smaller than one, so it's out.
Choice number three says x squared is equal to x. One equals one, so it stays too. Choice number four stays too. We haven't shown that either remaining statement is always true.

Now we try another easy number, two, and we check only choice numbers one and three. Two squared is four. Four is greater than two, so choice number one stays. Four isn't equal to two, so choice number three is out.

Choice number one and choice number four are left. Our examples haven't proved choice number one. So we ask: is choice number one always true? Three or ten would keep choice number one true, just like two.
To check whether choice number one can fail, we try a different kind of number. Zero, a big number, a negative number, or a fraction, as long as the restriction allows it. Zero isn't allowed here.
at: we try a different kind of number

slides.say: A negative number, minus two. Its square is four, and four is greater than minus two. So choice number one still stays.
at: four is greater than minus two

slides.say: A fraction, one half. One half times one half is one quarter. Is one quarter greater than or equal to one half? No, it's smaller. So choice number one isn't always true, and it's out.
Only choice number four is left. None of the above is necessarily true, so that's the answer.
at: Only choice number four is left

slides.say: And what if all the numbers we tried agree? That still doesn't prove always. We need a reason covering every allowed case, like in our earlier equation example. There the requested expression was always one and a half times the given eighteen, so its value was fixed.
Now let's see cannot be determined in numbers. Given, x plus y is six. What is x minus y?
Try x equals one and y equals five. One plus five is six, so they fit the given. But one minus five is minus four.
Now try x equals two and y equals four. Two plus four is six, so this pair fits too. Two minus four is minus two.
Both pairs fit the same given, but the requested answers are different. So the given doesn't fix x minus y. It cannot be determined. Two different results are enough to show that.

So, when do I plug in numbers? When there's an expression with a letter and the choices are numbers. When there are letters in the choices. When the amount doesn't matter, like in a ratio. And when there are more letters than equations.
at: when do I plug in numbers

slides.say: And how? First, check every restriction. Then choose an easy allowed number, often zero, and say why before you use it. See which choices it rules out. If more than one is left, try another easy number, and check only those.
at: Then choose an easy allowed number
If more than one is left

slides.say: Don't cross out none of the above or cannot be determined just because your examples agreed. Test a different kind of allowed number, or explain why the result must stay the same. And remember, it's your safety net.
at: Don't cross out none of the above

slides.say: It's the most important technique on the exam, so practice it a lot. Now let's see it in sample questions. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
